candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 37 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 38 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 39 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 40 not required. 41
candidates.context: This guidance revises the guidance for industry Determining Whether to Submit an ANDA or a 31 505(b)(2) Application issued in May 2019. When final, this guidance will replace the May 2019 32 guidance. Changes from the 2019 version include providing additional information on 33 duplicates and eligibility for approval under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act, as well as other 34 updates that are intended to clarify FDA’s recommendations to industry. 35 1 This guidance has been prepared by the Office of Generic Drugs (OGD) in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research at the Food and Drug Administration.

candidates.statement: The Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act of 1984 (Public Law 98-417) 44 (Hatch-Waxman Amendments) added sections 505(b)(2) and 505(j) to the FD&C Act, which 45 describes abbreviated approval pathways under the FD&C Act for drug products regulated by the 46 Agency. The Hatch-Waxman Amendments reflect Congress’s efforts to balance the need to 47 “make available more low cost generic drugs by establishing a generic drug approval procedure” 48 with new incentives for drug development in the form of exclusivities and patent term 49 extensions. 2 With the passage of the Hatch-Waxman Amendments, the FD&C Act describes 50 different routes for obtaining approval of two broad categories of drug applications: new drug 51 applications (NDAs) and abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs). 3

candidates.statement: As discussed in section II of this guidance, section 505(j) of the FD&C Act, together with its 107 implementing regulations, generally requires that an ANDA demonstrate that the proposed 108 generic drug product and the applicable RLD are the same with respect to their active 109 ingredient(s), dosage form, route of administration, strength, conditions of use, and labeling 110 (with certain exceptions). 15 An ANDA must also include sufficient information (1) to 111 demonstrate that the proposed drug product is bioequivalent to the RLD 16 and (2) to ensure the 112 drug’s identity, strength, quality, and purity. Consistent with any statutory provisions related to 113 the exclusivity of and patents listed for the RLD in FDA’s Approved Drug Products With 114 Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations (the Orange Book), FDA must approve an ANDA unless 115 there is insufficient evidence that these requirements are met. 17 An ANDA relies on the 116 Agency’s finding of safety and effectiveness for an RLD and, as a result, that ANDA may be 117 approved without submission of the same type and extent of information as is required for an 118 NDA to establish the safety and effectiveness of the proposed drug product. 18
candidates.context: Also, as discussed in section II above, an ANDA may contain certain types of differences from 121 an RLD (e.g., a change approved in response to a suitability petition or other permissible 122 differences, such as certain differences in inactive ingredients, labeling, or container closure 123 systems), as long as clinical investigations are not necessary to establish the safety or 124 effectiveness of the drug product proposed in the ANDA. 125

candidates.statement: The regulations at 21 CFR 314.94(a)(8)(iv) recognize that certain differences in labeling between 432 generic drug products and RLDs may be appropriate because the generic drug product and the 433 RLD are produced or distributed by different manufacturers. 76 For example, such differences 434 may include “differences in expiration date, formulation, bioavailability, or pharmacokinetics, 435 labeling revisions made to comply with current FDA labeling guidelines or other guidance, or 436 omission of an indication or other aspect of labeling protected by patent or accorded 437 exclusivity.” 77 Although the regulations indicate that these identified examples are not the only 438 acceptable differences in labeling between the generic drug product and the RLD, certain 439 differences in labeling will determine whether the proposed drug product should be submitted in 440 an ANDA or a 505(b)(2) application. For example, an ANDA is not appropriate if the proposed 441 drug product would have a new indication or a new dosing regimen as compared to the RLD 442 (e.g., a proposed drug product would be administered once daily even though the RLD is labeled 443 for administration twice daily). 78

candidates.statement: FDA reviews differences in labeling as part of the ANDA review process. If the differences in 446 labeling between the drug products are such that they would require clinical investigations to 447 establish the safety or effectiveness of the proposed drug product or are significant enough that 448 the labeling no longer satisfies the same labeling requirement, an ANDA would not be 449 appropriate for approval of the proposed drug product, and the applicant should instead consider 450 submitting a 505(b)(2) application. In reference to labeling carve-outs as discussed in section 451 IV.B.3.c of this guidance, FDA considers whether an ANDA drug product that omits the 452 protected information from its labeling would be rendered less safe or effective than the RLD for 453 its remaining nonprotected conditions of use. 79

candidates.statement: If an applicant is developing a drug product that is intended to have the same active 459 ingredient(s), conditions of use, route of administration, dosage form, strength, and (with certain 460 permissible differences) labeling as an RLD and has questions about whether the proposed drug 461 product would be appropriate for submission in an ANDA, the applicant can submit controlled 462 correspondence 80 to OGD or request a pre-ANDA meeting with OGD. Controlled 463 correspondence is appropriate if an applicant has a specific and targeted inquiry about the 464 generic drug development process. A pre-ANDA meeting is appropriate for a prospective 465 applicant seeking advice from the Agency on a particular matter that would fall outside the scope 466 of controlled correspondence. 81 Requests for pre-ANDA meetings should be submitted 467 electronically through the CDER Direct NextGen Collaboration Portal. 82

REQUESTING ASSISTANCE FROM FDA 457 If an applicant is developing a drug product that has a different route of administration, dosage 470 form, or strength, or active ingredient (in a drug product with more than one active ingredient) 471 than the RLD and the difference is the subject of an approved suitability petition, the applicant 472 can submit controlled correspondence to OGD with questions about developing the drug 473 pursuant to the approved suitability petition. 83
